title: Exhaust smell in cabin
h1: Why do I smell exhaust fumes inside my car?
metaDesc: Smell exhaust fumes inside your car? It can mean carbon monoxide. Answer a few questions to see how urgent it is and where the fumes are coming from.
synonyms: exhaust smell when heater is on
car smells like exhaust when idling
intro: Exhaust fumes inside the car always deserve attention, because exhaust carries carbon monoxide, a gas you can't smell or see that can make you sick or worse. Sometimes the fumes are just from traffic around you, but often your own exhaust is leaking or being drawn in. Answer the questions below to see how urgent it is and what to do.
safety: If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car. Get medical advice even if they start to feel better.
Never run the engine inside a garage that's attached to a house, even with the garage door open.
If you're parked with the engine running in snow, make sure the tailpipe is clear of snow first.
If the exhaust suddenly gets much louder and the fumes inside get stronger, pull over, turn off the engine and get out.
Keep a portable carbon monoxide detector in the car until the leak is repaired. It can warn you, but it doesn't fix the leak.

q_symptoms.q: Does anyone in the car have a headache, dizziness, nausea, unusual sleepiness or confusion?
q_symptoms.help: These are early signs of carbon monoxide exposure. Carbon monoxide has no smell, so you can be affected even when the exhaust smell seems mild.

q_when.q: When do you notice the fumes most?

opts.a: In heavy traffic or behind other vehicles, and it clears on an open road
When the rear hatch, tailgate, trunk or back windows are open
When parked with the engine running, especially in snow or a garage
Most of the time, whatever the traffic

q_noise.q: Have you noticed any new sound from the exhaust or engine?

opts.a: The exhaust is louder, rumbling, roaring or rattling underneath
A ticking or puffing sound from the engine, loudest when cold

result.title: Treat this as possible carbon monoxide exposure
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn off the engine, get everyone out into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car.
if: Even if symptoms improve in fresh air, follow the 911 dispatcher's advice and get checked. Carbon monoxide effects can linger, especially for children, pregnant people and anyone with heart or lung problems.
Don't use the car again until a shop has found and fixed the source. Have it towed or call a mechanic who comes to you.
result.why: Exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which you can't see or smell. It replaces oxygen in your blood and can cause headaches, dizziness and confusion before you realize anything is wrong. Symptoms in the car mean enough is getting in to be dangerous.

causes.name: Exhaust leak under the car or at the engine
causes.clues: A louder exhaust, a rattle, or a smell that's there whatever the traffic.

causes.name: Blocked tailpipe or running in an enclosed space
causes.clues: The car was idling in snow, a garage or another tight space.

causes.name: Fumes drawn in through an open hatch or bad seal
causes.clues: The rear hatch or windows were open, or the rear seals are damaged.

shop: Exhaust system leak inspection on a lift
Body seal and rear hatch seal inspection

result.title: You may be smelling other vehicles' exhaust
result.now: Switch the climate control to recirculate in heavy traffic and when following trucks or older vehicles, then switch back to fresh air on open roads.
if: If the smell continues on open roads with no traffic around, your own car may be leaking. Pull over when it's safe, get into fresh air and don't use the car again until the exhaust has been checked. Have it towed or call a mechanic who comes to you.

If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car. Get medical advice even if they start to feel better.
If your exhaust sounds louder than usual, or you hear a new rattle underneath, your own exhaust may be leaking. Don't keep driving it until it's checked.
result.why: In fresh-air mode the car pulls in air from just in front of the windshield, so fumes from the vehicle ahead come straight in. Recirculate mode keeps reusing the cabin air. If the smell comes and goes with traffic and clears on open roads, the source is probably outside your car, but a leak of your own can't be ruled out without a check.

causes.name: Fumes from nearby vehicles
causes.clues: Worse in stop-and-go traffic, tunnels or behind diesel trucks.
causes.against: If you smell it on empty roads, this is less likely.

causes.name: Small leak in your own exhaust
causes.clues: The smell is there even with no other cars around.

you: Notice whether the smell disappears on open roads.
Try recirculate mode in traffic and see if the smell stops.

result.title: Exhaust may be getting pulled in through the back of the car
result.now: Keep the rear hatch, trunk and back windows closed while driving, and have the rear seals and exhaust checked within a few days.
if: Avoid driving with the hatch open. If you can't avoid it for a short trip, open the front windows and set the fan to fresh air on high.
If the smell is there even with everything closed, don't drive it until the exhaust and seals are checked.

If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car. Get medical advice even if they start to feel better.
result.why: As a car moves, low air pressure forms behind it and can pull exhaust toward the back. With a hatch or window open, or a worn seal, those fumes get sucked into the cabin. Wagons, SUVs and hatchbacks are especially prone to this.

causes.name: Driving with the rear hatch or windows open
causes.clues: The smell only appears when something at the back is open.

causes.name: Worn or damaged hatch or trunk seal
causes.clues: Torn or flattened rubber, or water also getting into the trunk.

causes.name: Exhaust leak near the rear or a damaged tailpipe
causes.clues: A louder exhaust, or the tailpipe is bent or points up toward the bumper.

you: Check the rubber seals around the hatch or trunk for tears.
Look at the tailpipe for damage or holes.
shop: Smoke test of the rear body openings

result.title: Exhaust may be building up around the car because it can't escape
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn off the engine and get into fresh air. Before running the engine again, clear snow from the tailpipe and around the car, or move it out of any enclosed space with the engine off.
if: If the smell continues outdoors with a clear tailpipe, don't use the car. There may be an exhaust leak, so have it towed or call a mechanic who comes to you.

If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car. Get medical advice even if they start to feel better.
result.why: When the tailpipe is buried in snow or the car is in a garage or tight space, exhaust gathers around the car and seeps in through vents and seals. Carbon monoxide can reach dangerous levels quickly, even when the smell seems faint.

causes.name: Tailpipe blocked by snow
causes.clues: The car was parked in or near a snowbank, or snow built up while idling.

causes.name: Idling in an enclosed space
causes.clues: The car was running in a garage, parking structure or other tight space.

causes.name: Exhaust leak made worse while idling
causes.clues: The smell is there outdoors with a clear tailpipe.

you: With the engine off, clear snow from the tailpipe and the area around the car.
Never warm the car up inside a garage, even with the door open.

result.title: The exhaust system may be leaking under the car
result.now: Don't use the car until it's repaired. Have it towed or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual). A mechanic who comes to you can also inspect the exhaust.
if: If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car. Get medical advice even if they start to feel better.
If part of the exhaust is hanging or dragging, don't move the car at all until it's secured or towed.
result.why: A louder exhaust plus fumes inside usually means exhaust is escaping before it reaches the tailpipe, often under the cabin floor. It can seep in through gaps in the floor and seals, carrying carbon monoxide you can't smell.

causes.name: Rusted or cracked exhaust pipe or muffler
causes.clues: A deep rumble or roar, worse when accelerating, especially on an older car or in salted-road areas.

causes.name: Failed exhaust joint, gasket or flex pipe
causes.clues: A puffing or rasping sound under the middle of the car.

causes.name: Broken hanger or damage from road debris
causes.clues: A rattle or clunk underneath, or the exhaust hangs lower than before.

you: With the engine off and cool, look under the car for hanging pipes or obvious holes.
shop: Exhaust system leak inspection on a lift

result.title: The exhaust may be leaking near the engine (exhaust manifold or gasket)
result.now: Don't use the car until the leak is fixed, because the fumes can be pulled in through the vents. Have it towed or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual).
if: If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car. Get medical advice even if they start to feel better.
If you also smell burning oil or see smoke under the hood, keep away from the engine and call for help.
result.why: The exhaust manifold collects exhaust right at the engine, close to where the ventilation system draws in outside air. A crack or a failed gasket there makes a ticking or puffing sound and can send fumes straight through the vents, especially with the heat or fan on.

causes.name: Failed exhaust manifold gasket
causes.clues: Ticking that's loudest on a cold start and quiets as the engine warms up.

causes.name: Cracked exhaust manifold
causes.clues: A ticking that gets louder over time, sometimes with black soot marks near the engine.

causes.name: Broken or loose manifold bolts or studs
causes.clues: Common on older engines, often with soot around one corner of the manifold.

result.title: Exhaust may be leaking somewhere and needs to be found before you use the car
result.now: Avoid using the car until the source is found. Have a mechanic inspect it where it's parked, or have it towed to a shop, so nobody has to breathe the fumes on the way.
if: If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car. Get medical advice even if they start to feel better.
If the exhaust gets louder or you hear a new rattle underneath, mention it to the shop. It helps them find the leak.
If the smell only shows up in heavy traffic and clears completely on open roads, it may be outside air, but have the exhaust checked to be sure. If it doesn't clear, don't keep driving it.
result.why: Fumes inside with no obvious noise can come from a small leak, a damaged seal, or a hole where exhaust can seep into the body. Even small leaks can let in carbon monoxide, and carbon monoxide has no smell, so a faint exhaust smell doesn't mean a small dose.

causes.name: Small exhaust leak
causes.clues: Black soot marks around an exhaust joint, or a faint puff you can hear at idle.

causes.name: Damaged body seal, floor plug or rust hole
causes.clues: Missing rubber plugs in the floor, rust holes, or water also getting in.

causes.name: Engine running poorly
causes.clues: A check engine light, rough running or a strong fuel smell in the exhaust.

you: Note whether the smell is worse when stopped, when accelerating or with the heat on.
If you have a battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm, it can warn you if fumes are getting in.
